chief_complaint: incontinence, urinary tract infections, and autonomic dysreflexia in paraplegic patient with high bladder pressures
hpi_details: 39M with T6 paraplegia presenting with urinary leakage between self-catheterizations where urodynamics reveal detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, poor bladder compliance, and elevated detrusor storage pressures (>40 cmH2O) requiring intradetrusor OnabotulinumtoxinA injections.
ideas: He thinks the disrupted nerve signals from his spinal cord injury are making his bladder spasm uncontrollably against a closed sphincter.
concerns: He is frightened that the dangerous blood pressure spikes during his bladder spasms will trigger a stroke while he is alone.
expectations: He hopes to get scheduled for bladder Botox injections so his bladder relaxes and stops leaking between catheterizations.
pmh: T6 spinal cord injury with paraplegia

clinical_knowledge.topic: Neurogenic Bladder Spinal Cord Injury evaluation and management
core_concepts: High detrusor storage pressures and poor compliance can cause reflux, hydronephrosis, recurrent infection, and renal deterioration.

In people with spinal cord injury at or above T6, autonomic dysreflexia is a hypertensive emergency; sit the patient upright, remove tight clothing, identify and relieve triggers such as bladder obstruction, and seek emergency care.
Use urinalysis and culture only when symptoms or systemic features suggest infection; bacteriuria or cloudy urine alone is common with catheterization and should not prompt antibiotics.

Clean intermittent catheterization and pressure-lowering therapy are individualized. Botulinum toxin can improve storage but may worsen retention, so ability to catheterize and follow-up are essential.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: incontinence, urinary tract infections, and autonomic dysreflexia in paraplegic patient with high bladder pressures
T6 paraplegia, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, poor compliance, and storage pressure above 40 cm H2O place upper tracts at risk.
Measure blood pressure during symptoms, assess catheter patency and residuals, renal function, and upper-tract surveillance.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Neurogenic Bladder Spinal Cord Injury.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Urinary tract infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Missing autonomic dysreflexia, severe hypertension, retention, pyelonephritis/urosepsis, or acute kidney injury.
Giving botulinum toxin without confirming a safe catheterization plan and renal-aware follow-up.
management_principles: Urgently assess and treat autonomic dysreflexia or sepsis; check drainage immediately when bladder distension is suspected.
Refer to neuro-urology for pressure-lowering strategy, catheterization review, renal ultrasound/creatinine surveillance, and repeat urodynamics when indicated.
Culture and treat symptomatic infection based on results, renal function, and local guidance; avoid routine suppressive antibiotics.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Neurogenic Bladder Spinal Cord Injury.
reference_soap.assessment: High-risk neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction from T6 injury with dangerous storage pressures and autonomic dysreflexia risk.
reference_soap.plan: Check blood pressure and bladder drainage now if dysreflexia symptoms occur; arrange urgent neuro-urology management to protect renal function. Treat only symptomatic, culture-supported infection and individualize pressure-lowering treatment.

teaching.diagnosis: High-risk neurogenic bladder due to spinal cord injury
teaching.one_liner: A man with T6 paraplegia has dyssynergia, poor compliance, and high storage pressures, creating renal and autonomic dysreflexia risk.
differentials: Bladder outlet obstruction from catheter malposition
Autonomic dysreflexia from another trigger (bowel impaction, skin ulcer)

must_ask.say: How often do you self-catheterize each day, and has that schedule changed recently?
Do you get pounding headaches, sweating, or flushing above your level of injury when your bladder is full?
Are you leaking urine between catheterizations, and how much?
Have you had repeated bladder infections, cloudy urine, or fevers?

must_ask.objective: Level and completeness of spinal cord injury
must_ask.say: Can you remind me the level of your spinal cord injury and whether it's complete or incomplete?

history.answer: Ever since my spinal cord injury, I do clean self-catheterization, but over the last few weeks urine has been leaking out between my cath times.
The leaking between catheterizations is my main problem; I do not void on my own at all.
The leakage started gradually about a month ago and has gotten steadily more frequent.
I cannot initiate urination or pass urine voluntarily, so I rely entirely on catheterizing myself every four hours.
I do not feel normal bladder fullness anymore, but when I cath, I usually drain around 350 to 400 mL.
history.topic: Incomplete emptying and post void dribbling

history.answer: I cannot urinate without a catheter, but my lower belly does not feel painfully bloated because I have no sensation down there.
history.topic: Urinary retention and lower abdominal swelling

history.answer: I catheterize about five to six times during the day and once before going to bed, never waking up overnight just to cath.
I do not feel a normal urge to pee, but right before the leakage happens, I get a sudden tight feeling and goosebumps on my arms.
No, coughing, sneezing, or laughing does not make me leak.
It leaks enough to soak through my underwear, so I have had to wear absorbent pads every day, which really limits my independence.
I have no pain with urination, but I have had cloudy, foul-smelling urine and three treated urinary infections over the past four months, though no fever today.

history.answer: I have complete loss of feeling and movement below my mid-chest from my T6 injury, and I manage my bowels using a digital routine every other morning.
No, I keep a strict bowel routine and have not been constipated or had stool impaction.
I drink about two liters of water a day, avoid coffee, and try to stop drinking liquids after eight in the evening.
No, I have not taken any decongestants, cold medicines, antidepressants, or water pills.
I have no history of diabetes, stroke, or Parkinson disease, just my spine surgery following my cord injury three years ago.
I have never had pelvic trauma or urethral strictures, and I insert the catheter smoothly without resistance.
I use sterile, single-use hydrophilic catheters six times a day, washing my hands thoroughly and using clean technique every time.
When the leaking happens or if my bladder gets too full, I suddenly get a throbbing headache, profuse sweating on my face, and flushed skin above my chest.
I had a T6 complete spinal cord injury from a motorcycle accident three years ago, leaving me paralyzed from the mid-chest down.
I have no other chronic medical illnesses besides the paraplegia and neurogenic bladder.
I had spinal stabilization surgery with instrumentation three years ago right after the accident; no other surgeries since.
I am not taking any prescription medications or over-the-counter supplements right now.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I do not drink alcohol.
I work remotely in computer programming, live in an accessible apartment with my partner, and remain as active as I can.
There is no family history of kidney or bladder diseases.
I have erectile dysfunction since my injury, but I am in a supportive relationship and we adapt.
I think the nerve signals from my spinal cord injury are misfiring and causing my bladder to spasm violently between catheterizations.
Whenever my bladder gets full, my head pounds and my blood pressure spikes so high that I'm terrified I'll have a stroke.
I'm hoping we can set up the Botox injections today so my bladder finally relaxes and stops leaking between caths.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 72/min, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, seated comfortably in a wheelchair, no diaphoresis, facial flushing, or acute distress.
Soft, non-tender, non-distended; no fullness or dullness over the suprapubic area; bladder is not palpable.
Tympanic throughout the abdomen with no dullness to percussion over the suprapubic region.
Normal external male genitalia; urethral meatus is clear without discharge or excoriation.
Normal anal sphincter resting tone is absent; absent voluntary sphincter contraction; prostate is normal size, smooth, non-tender, with no nodules.
Flaccid paraplegia with grade 0/5 motor strength throughout both lower extremities bilaterally; upper extremities are 5/5 throughout.
Absent light touch and pinprick sensation below the T6 dermatome, including the perineal and perianal regions.
Bilateral patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 3+ with bilateral extensor plantar responses (Babinski positive); bulbocavernosus reflex is intact.
No sacral or ischial pressure ulcers, rashes, or skin breakdown seen.
